items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Goldman Sachs (George Lee)
items.title: Cost to orbit fell 98% in a generation — Goldman sees a $1.8T space economy by 2035
items.idea: Goldman's George Lee frames the space economy as structurally larger than a speculative tech theme: the cost to carry 1kg to low Earth orbit fell from roughly $65,400 on the Space Shuttle to about $1,500 on Falcon Heavy. That collapse is opening commercial markets in comms, Earth observation, direct-to-cell and orbital compute that could not clear the hurdle rate a decade ago, and Goldman pegs the global space economy at $1.8 trillion by 2035.
items.angle: Same cost-curve pattern as solar and lithium-ion — once launch cost crosses a threshold, capital starts treating space like the internet: infrastructure, not novelty. The second-derivative trade (ground stations, sats, insurance, orbital compute) is worth mapping beyond SpaceX itself.
items.tweetA: $65,400 to $1,500. That's the cost per kg to orbit, Shuttle to Falcon Heavy — a 98% collapse in one generation. Every 'space is a bubble' take ignores that we've seen this exact curve before, in solar panels and lithium cells.
items.tweetB: Everyone's arguing whether AI capex is overbuilt. Nobody's asking the same question about orbit. Goldman's $1.8T-by-2035 number assumes launch costs keep falling — the same assumption every AI capex bull is making about compute costs. Same bet, different frontier.

items.title: Credit spreads at cycle lows, 30yr yields at cycle highs — the last time that happened was 2022
items.idea: Short-term equity positioning looks too aggressive: Monday's selloff had zero mean reversion into the close and every session handoff (overnight, London, cash open) failed to find a bid. Meanwhile credit spreads sit at cycle lows while 30-year yields sit at cycle highs — a divergence that signals inflation risk dominating over recession risk, since spreads would be widening (not tightening) if recession were the market's real fear.
items.angle: The credit market and the bond market are both voting for the same regime call, which matters more for positioning than any single equity print — it argues against re-fighting the 2023-24 'Fed cuts into a recession' trade.
items.tweetA: Credit spreads at cycle lows. 30yr yield at cycle highs. Those two things are NOT supposed to move together — spreads widen when recession is the fear, they tighten when inflation is. Credit and duration are both voting for 2022, not 2020.
items.tweetB: If you're still positioned for the Fed cutting into a recession, the credit market disagrees with you. IG and HY spreads haven't moved. All the stress is in duration, not credit quality. That's a specific, tradeable signal, not a vibe.

items.title: SOFR futures are pricing dovish — but only temporarily, per Carson Group
items.idea: Markets currently price the doves as having the upper hand in SOFR futures, but Carson Group's Sonu Varghese notes that's likely temporary: if policy holds unchanged while nominal GDP and inflation run hot amid huge fiscal deficits and the AI buildout, the Fed may eventually be forced into a more restrictive stance than what's currently priced.
items.angle: This is a repricing risk sitting in short-end vol, not equities — if SOFR unwinds its dovish pricing, that's the tightening event equities haven't discounted at all right now.
items.tweetA: SOFR futures are pricing a dovish Fed. The fiscal deficit and the AI capex boom are pricing a hot economy. Both cannot be right for long. When the front end catches up to the back end's inflation story, that's the real risk-off event — not another Hormuz headline.
items.tweetB: The market keeps repricing recession fears out of the front end. Nobody's repricing the chance the Fed has to hike back. That's the trade nobody's positioned for and the one with the fattest tails right now.

items.title: 10y10y forward yields are rising fastest exactly where debt is highest and politics is worst
items.idea: 10y10y forward bond yields — the market's price of where the 10-year sits a decade out — are rising globally, but rising most where the stock of government debt is high and political dysfunction is acute. This is a solvency and credibility repricing, not a growth-expectations story.
items.angle: Lines up directly with the Goldman 'AI financing is now a supply problem for the bond market' framing (item 11) and Thiel's rotation to energy/utilities (item 15) — three independent sources converging on term premium, not the Fed, as the driver of the long end.
items.tweetA: 10y10y forward yields aren't rising because growth expectations changed. They're rising fastest exactly where debt-to-GDP is worst and politics is most broken. The bond market isn't pricing inflation. It's pricing solvency.
items.tweetB: Line up Robin Brooks' debt-and-dysfunction map against Goldman's call that AI financing is now a bond-market supply problem. Two different desks, same conclusion: term premium is driving the long end. Rate cuts won't fix this.

items.title: CME Bitcoin large specs near-record long — historically a marker of lows, not tops
items.idea: CME Bitcoin large speculators remain near-record long: net positioning is at 18.2% of open interest, just below June's 20.6% record. Similar positioning extremes have historically clustered around major longer-term BTC lows rather than tops.
items.angle: Crowded long futures positioning sitting inside a broad risk-off tape is a contrarian setup worth flagging — the historical pattern argues against reading 'record long' as euphoria right now.
items.tweetA: CME BTC large specs are at 18.2% of open interest — near June's 20.6% record long. Historically that positioning extreme has clustered around BTC LOWS, not tops. Everyone reads 'record long' as euphoria. The historical pattern says the opposite.
items.tweetB: Crypto is getting dragged lower with everything else in this bond-yield selloff, but futures positioning doesn't look like a top setup — it looks like the pattern that's marked bottoms before. Worth watching whether spot decouples from the macro tape here.

items.title: Equity and bond fund flows now exceed 2021 levels
items.idea: US equity fund flows (and bond fund flows, and ETFs) are robust at levels now exceeding 2021 — the peak of the last euphoric flow cycle. This is happening at the same time forward earnings are separately hitting record highs across large, mid and small caps (item 7), not purely off multiple expansion.
items.angle: 2021's flow peak was chasing multiple expansion; this year's flow peak is chasing an actual earnings record — a materially different setup even though the flow intensity looks the same, which matters for how a crack would actually play out.
items.tweetA: Fund flows into equities and bonds are now above 2021 levels. Everyone remembers what happened after 2021 flows peaked. But 2021's flows were chasing multiple expansion. This year's are chasing an actual earnings record. Same intensity, different setup.
items.tweetB: 2021 vs now: identical flow intensity, opposite earnings backdrop. That doesn't mean this ends better — it means if it cracks, it's an earnings-disappointment story, not a multiple-compression story. Watch guidance season, not the Fed, for the real risk.

items.title: Forward earnings hit record highs across large, mid AND small caps simultaneously
items.idea: Forward earnings are rising to record highs across the S&P 500 LargeCaps, S&P 400 MidCaps and S&P 600 SmallCaps at the same time — breadth in the earnings data, not just mega-cap AI names carrying the index.
items.angle: This is the direct bull counterweight to the 'narrow market' and rising-correlation warnings in items 8 and 14 — worth weighing both against each other rather than picking one narrative.
items.tweetA: Forward earnings at record highs in large caps, mid caps, AND small caps simultaneously. This isn't 7 stocks propping up an index. Short 'narrow market' logic alone doesn't hold up against this data.
items.tweetB: Small cap forward earnings just hit a record alongside megacap. Yet the Russell is down 1.3% today on bond yields, tracking Nasdaq lower. That's not an earnings problem — it's a discount-rate problem hitting every cap size at once.

items.title: China quietly rebuilt its oil bunker in July — but it's storage, not demand
items.idea: China is estimated to have added roughly 200,000 bpd to crude inventories in July, reversing the May-June drawdown even as the Hormuz crisis continued. It entered the Iran conflict sitting on an estimated 1.4 billion barrels of commercial and strategic crude and, even after drawing down during the worst of the disruption, still holds an estimated 1.2 billion barrels — a massive shock absorber. Refinery runs stayed subdued, meaning the imported barrels are going into storage rather than being consumed.
items.angle: China's stockpile size means it can absorb a Hormuz shock for a long time without a demand-driven price spike from Beijing — but this 'resilience' is passive storage, not economic strength, which cuts against any bullish China-demand narrative riding on the same headline.
items.tweetA: China sits on 1.2 billion barrels of crude and just added 200k bpd back to the pile in July. That's not a demand recovery — refinery runs stayed weak, so it's barrels going into the warehouse, not the economy. Don't confuse Beijing restocking with Beijing growing.
items.tweetB: The bull case for oil right now leans entirely on Hormuz. The bear case is sitting in a Chinese tank farm: 1.2B barrels of dry powder that can absorb any supply shock for months. Whoever's short oil purely on 'Hormuz forever' is ignoring the guy with the biggest storage tank on earth.

items.title: Trump says no talks with Iran are scheduled — Hormuz risk is becoming permanent, not an event
items.idea: Trump now insists there are no talks or negotiations underway with Iran and none scheduled; the June MOU has expired with no extension planned. Iran's lead negotiator says the strait will not reopen until the US lifts its port blockade, releases frozen assets, removes oil sanctions and ends military operations. The UAE has now cut trade, commercial and financial ties with Iran after alleging Iran fired two ballistic missiles toward its territory (Tehran denies it), and a separate vessel exiting Hormuz was struck by a projectile. Brent is holding above $91/bbl.
items.angle: The gap between US and Iranian positions has moved from 'negotiating distance' to structurally incompatible demands — worth treating the Hormuz risk premium as a permanent feature to size into energy and shipping exposure, not an event to trade around.
items.tweetA: Trump: no talks with Iran, none scheduled. Iran: the strait doesn't reopen until the blockade ends. Those aren't two sides negotiating — that's two sides that stopped negotiating and are calling it a negotiation. The market is still pricing this as an event. It's becoming a regime.
items.tweetB: The UAE just cut financial ties with Iran over an alleged missile launch. That's a Gulf state — not Washington — escalating first. When regional players start pricing this as permanent before the US does, that's usually the more reliable signal. Worth a structural look at energy/shipping exposure, not a spike trade.

items.title: AI companies have already borrowed more in 2026 than all of 2025 — and credit is pricing the risk equity vol isn't
items.idea: AI-linked companies have raised roughly $489 billion across investment-grade, high-yield and leveraged loans so far this year, already above the full $322 billion raised in all of 2025, while total USD IG issuance has pushed past $1.5 trillion. The SOX reversed at its 50-day moving average and broke below near-term support. CDS spreads across several hyperscalers have widened even as Nasdaq volatility (VXN) stays subdued — a gap between credit and equity vol pricing the same risk very differently. BTIG notes price and breadth have diverged in opposite directions 57 times this year, tying the highest annual total in three decades.
items.angle: Credit is pricing more risk into the AI trade than equity vol is right now — that CDS-vs-VXN gap is the more useful leading indicator than SPX or SOX price action alone, and it's a very specific, checkable divergence to track day to day.
items.tweetA: AI companies have already borrowed $489B this year — more than ALL of 2025's $322B — and hyperscaler CDS is widening while Nasdaq vol stays asleep. Credit is pricing this risk. Equity vol isn't. One of those two markets is about to be very wrong, and it's not usually credit.
items.tweetB: Price and breadth have diverged in opposite directions 57 times this year — already tying the highest annual count in three decades. So far that's just meant rotation, chair to chair. The risk is what happens the day everyone tries to leave the room through the same door.

items.title: The FCC moved Disney/ABC's license renewal clock up 2-5 years — Disney is suing over it
items.idea: The FCC ordered 8 ABC-owned TV stations to seek license renewal between two and five years before their 8-year terms (under 47 U.S.C. §307(c)) actually expire. Disney and ABC sued on August 18, alleging the early-review order is retaliation for editorial and entertainment content, violating the First Amendment. The suit lands days after the FCC voted 2-1 to lift the 39% national TV ownership cap.
items.angle: This is a template — regulatory timing itself, not an outright license denial, is being used as leverage over content, which every media/broadcast owner now has to price into M&A and programming decisions, and it directly intersects with the ownership-cap deregulation trade in station-group M&A.
items.tweetA: The FCC didn't revoke Disney's license. It just moved the renewal clock up 2-5 years. That's the whole play — you don't need to punish speech, you just need the compliance and legal spend to start early enough that every newsroom gets the message. This is a template, not a one-off.
items.tweetB: Same week the FCC lifts the 39% ownership cap AND accelerates ABC's license review. Deregulation for M&A, discretion as a leash for content — that's not a contradiction, that's the strategy. Every broadcast buyer now has to price 'FCC discretion' into deal terms.

items.title: Third straight losing session for SPX — Rosenberg flags the 30yr breakout preceded the dot-com peak by 3 months
items.idea: SPX fell 0.7% for a third consecutive session, the Nasdaq lost 1.3%, the Russell 2000 fell 1.3%, while the less tech-heavy Dow held up better at -0.2% as the SOX tumbled 5.0%. The 30-year Treasury yield hit its highest level since 2007 (~5.3%) and the 10-year its highest since January 2025 (~4.74%). David Rosenberg specifically notes the 30-year yield's prior breakout in 2000 led the dot-com bull market peak by three months.
items.angle: Rosenberg's historical parallel is the sharpest, most checkable thing buried in the wrap — a specific analog worth flagging on its own rather than the generic 'yields are high' framing everyone else is using today.
items.tweetA: Rosenberg just pointed out the 30yr yield breaking to a multi-decade high preceded the dot-com peak by exactly three months in 2000. We're at that same kind of breakout level right now. Nobody's talking about that specific parallel — everyone's just saying 'yields are high.'
items.tweetB: Third straight down day for SPX, and the Dow (-0.2%) is outperforming Nasdaq (-1.3%) by more than a point for the third day running. That rotation — megacap tech underperforming the value-heavy Dow — is the tell this is a duration story, not a growth-scare story.

items.title: Falling single-stock volatility is quietly removing the S&P 500's internal shock absorber
items.idea: Bloomberg's Michael Ball flags that falling single-stock volatility (low dispersion) is eroding one of the S&P 500's key diversification cushions. The real signal to watch isn't dispersion itself but whether implied correlation starts rising with the index — which would mean stocks are increasingly riding the same 'Goldilocks' assumptions (resilient growth, Fed on hold, easing energy, no Iran escalation) simultaneously, so any single disappointment hits the whole index at once.
items.angle: Pair this directly with item 13's Dow/Nasdaq rotation and item 10's Iran escalation — two of the four Goldilocks assumptions this piece names (oil, Iran) already cracked today, which is the live trigger case this framework describes.
items.tweetA: The chart nobody's watching: implied correlation, not the VIX. Low single-stock vol has been masking index-level risk for months. The day correlation starts rising WITH the index — not against it — is the day 'diversified' S&P 500 exposure stops meaning anything for a week or two.
items.tweetB: Four assumptions are doing all the work in this market right now: growth holds, the Fed stays on hold, oil eases, Iran doesn't escalate. Today two of those four (oil, Iran) already cracked. That's the exact setup this correlation piece is warning about, playing out in real time.

items.title: The AI buildout is now bigger than the debt stock of several G10 economies
items.idea: Estimates put the AI buildout at $2-3.6 trillion in infrastructure spending, plus roughly another $3 trillion in off-balance-sheet commitments (leases, power contracts, chip commitments) — a sum larger than the entire government debt stock of several G10 economies, now competing directly with sovereign issuance for the same pool of long-duration capital. Separately, the US diesel crack spread has blown through $100/bbl, and Korea's market is signaled to open down roughly 25% on a 'nasty read-through.'
items.angle: This quantifies exactly why AI capex became a rates story rather than a tech story — the diesel crack spread is a faster-moving, more real-economy inflation signal than headline CPI will show for months, and the Korea gap-down is a concrete overnight event to check first thing.
items.tweetA: The AI buildout is now larger than the entire government debt stock of several G10 countries. It's not competing with Big Tech's cash pile for capital anymore — it's competing with SOVEREIGNS. That's why the 30yr is breaking out. This was never just a tech story.
items.tweetB: Diesel crack spread just blew through $100/bbl. Nobody trades diesel cracks except energy desks, but diesel is the actual bloodstream of the physical economy — trucking, freight, ag. That number moves through the real economy months before it shows up in CPI. Watch it, not Brent.

items.title: Pending home sales just printed the second-lowest reading since 2001
items.idea: July pending home sales fell 2.3% m/m (vs. 0.0% est) to an index level of 71.2 — the second-lowest reading on record since 2001, behind only January's 70.9 — while y/y contract signings fell 2.5% (vs +1.1% est), the biggest annual drop since April 2025. The average 30-year mortgage rate rose from 6.43% to 6.66% within July alone, its highest in a year. All four US regions fell m/m; the West is down 7.1% y/y while the Midwest is the only region still positive y/y.
items.angle: This print landed the same day the 10yr and 30yr both hit fresh multi-year highs — housing is the real-economy confirmation that higher-for-longer duration is already biting, not a future risk to model.
items.tweetA: Pending home sales just printed the second-lowest reading since 2001 — worse than the depths of 2008. Mortgage rates went from 6.43% to 6.66% in a single month and housing just stopped. This isn't a forecast about what higher yields will do to the economy. It's already happening.
items.tweetB: The West is down 7.1% y/y in pending sales while the Midwest is still positive. That's not a national story, it's a high-cost-market story — exactly where rate sensitivity bites hardest. Worth watching CA/WA-exposed homebuilders and regional banks before the national data catches up.
